body: Ice can be many things at once.
Ice is land and not land; water and not water; air and also not air. Ice is material and amaterial;
the multiple psychic imaginaries of ice
I’m interested in how both material and imaginaries of ice intertine in questions around temperature and analyses of power relations.
This world has been historically and colonially sorted and separated into categories cold from hot, water from land, and Blackness from indigeneity, among other organizings and hierarchies
. Building from offerings and inferences in chapter 1, I insist that
ice pushes us to understand these categories as

Melting ice has become a spectacle on a global scale. The Arctic acts as a barometer for the pace of climate change. Drone images of calving glaciers and splitting ice sheets circulate widely in multiple forms of catastrophe media
questions of state sovereignty and property
. Capitalist enterprises emerge as new economies of traffic, and they are routed through shipping lanes where ice once withheld entrance.

. As discussed in the previous chapter, many of these ice transformations are taken up by scholars and experts contributing to conversations of the Anthropocene, an unofficial geologic epoch that finds human-induced change to the globe as heralding a new earthly time. Yet, enlisting Arc- tic spaces of ice as indicator of universalized human history and human futurity is not new nor innocent.

In this chapter, I trace an abridged racial history of ice with a focus on Arctic spaces and demonstrate the undeniable links to Bering Land Bridge postulations. Multiple statesanctioned plans overlapped in their attempts to remove freed Black people to the tropics of Africa and/or created a “domestic tropics” of the US South.

Alternatively, Anya Zilberstein has written that the transatlantic slave trade was utilized as a kind of “proof of concept” to disprove geographical determinism, that enslaved Africans could labor productively in geographies foreign to them.6 Zilberstein writes that racial theories of human difference on the basis of climate were built into the second half of the twentieth century. She writes that they “took on a much broader resonance in assumptions about the contemporary geography of economic development, underdevelopment, and the horizons of possibility captured in monolithic terms Global North and Global South.”7 I add to these critical conversations that the racialization and subject-making enacted in relation to
